section_summary: This section contains wartime reports from Bern on declining Japanese cocoon and silk production, including a translated German newspaper survey of the silk industries in Japan and Japanese-occupied China. The survey describes falling output, changes in silk processing and pricing, Japanese control of Chinese mills, and shrinking export markets. A separate confidential State Department memorandum considers Department of Justice inquiries concerning a possible Logan Act prosecution arising from Raoul E. Desvernine's attempted Japanese-American barter negotiations.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 897 reporting Japanese cocoon-production estimates
subfiles.about: Reports German press figures for Japanese cocoon production and the declining number of individual silk producers.
subfiles.summary: A Tokyo despatch published in the German press estimated Japan's autumn 1943 cocoon crop at 94,000 metric tons and total 1943 production at 205,000 metric tons, equal to the reported 1942 total. The number of individual producers had fallen by 104,000 to 1,120,000.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 7275: The silk industry in Japan and occupied China
subfiles.from: Hugh S. Fullerton, Counselor of Legation, for the U.S. Minister at Bern
subfiles.about: Transmits a translation of a German newspaper article on current conditions in the silk industries of Japan and occupied China.
subfiles.summary: The American Legation at Bern forwards a translation of an article published in the Kölnische Zeitung on February 4, 1944. The attached article concerns wartime conditions in the silk industries of Japan and Japanese-occupied China.

subfiles.title: Japanese Silk Industry
subfiles.from: Kölnische Zeitung, translated and transmitted by the American Legation at Bern
subfiles.to: Department of State, as enclosure to despatch no. 7275
subfiles.about: Surveys falling silk production, altered processing and prices in Japan, and Japanese control and contraction of the silk industry in occupied China.
subfiles.summary: Japanese cocoon production fell sharply after the loss of the United States market, while government policy emphasized quantity, simplified grades, and greatly expanded production of silk wool. Raw-silk prices rose with improved export opportunities to Manchuria and Indochina. In occupied China, production declined as Japanese authorities favored cotton, and the Kachu Company controlled most large mills and cocoon purchases. Stocks accumulated because of weak demand and inadequate shipping, while production in Guangdong also contracted.

subfiles.title: Duplicate despatch no. 7275: The silk industry in Japan and occupied China
subfiles.from: Hugh S. Fullerton, Counselor of Legation, for the U.S. Minister at Bern
subfiles.about: Duplicate copy transmitting a translation of a German newspaper article on silk production in Japan and occupied China.
subfiles.summary: This is another copy of despatch no. 7275 from the American Legation at Bern. It forwards the February 4, 1944 Kölnische Zeitung article concerning current conditions in the Japanese and occupied-Chinese silk industries.

subfiles.title: Duplicate enclosure: Japanese Silk Industry
subfiles.from: Kölnische Zeitung, translated and transmitted by the American Legation at Bern
subfiles.to: Department of State, as enclosure to despatch no. 7275
subfiles.about: Duplicate translation describing wartime changes in the Japanese and occupied-Chinese silk industries.
subfiles.summary: The duplicate enclosure records declining Japanese cocoon output, the prioritization of volume over quality, expanded silk-wool manufacture, and changing raw-silk prices and export outlets. It also describes the contraction of silk production in occupied China and the dominant position of the Kachu Company. Chinese mills faced strict size limits, small raw-silk stocks, weak demand, and shipping shortages.

subfiles.title: Strictly confidential memorandum on the possible Logan Act prosecution of Raoul E. Desvernine
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs; drafting notation FE:Salisbury:MJK
subfiles.about: Requests guidance on Department of Justice inquiries connected with a possible prosecution of Desvernine for unauthorized Japanese-American barter negotiations.
subfiles.summary: Justice Department representative Jesse Climenko examined State Department records concerning Raoul E. Desvernine's 1941 effort to arrange a Japanese-American barter transaction and raised the possibility of prosecution under the Logan Act. He asked whether confidential information from Dean Acheson's memorandum and the Secretary's telephone conversation with Jouett Shouse could be used to interrogate Desvernine, and whether Justice could approach Shouse. Hackworth recommended first asking Shouse about the matter and postponing a decision on using the information until his response was known.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 7039 reporting further decline in Japanese cocoon production
subfiles.from: Leland Harrison, U.S. Legation at Bern
subfiles.about: Relays a German press report on the falling number of Japanese silk producers and reduced cocoon output.
subfiles.summary: A Tokyo despatch published by the German press reported 995,000 Japanese silk producers, down from 1,114,000 in spring 1943, and cocoon production of approximately 23.7 million kan compared with 29.4 million kan the previous year. The decline in producers was attributed to the need to expand food production and abandon mulberry cultivation. Lower cocoon output was blamed on labor transfers to war industries and abnormally cold weather.
